paragraphs.heading: Rome's eastern half lives on
paragraphs.text: The Byzantine Empire, also called the Eastern Roman Empire, was the eastern part of the Roman Empire carrying on through late antiquity and the Middle Ages, with Constantinople as its centre. It outlasted the fall of the western half in the 5th century AD and kept going until the Ottoman Empire took Constantinople in 1453. The name Byzantine was only invented after the empire was gone. Its own people spoke of the Roman Empire and thought of themselves as Romans.

paragraphs.heading: Splitting the empire
paragraphs.text: In the 3rd century AD the Roman Empire was hit by outside threats and inner crises, and regional armies began naming their own generals emperor. One of these, Diocletian, decided the state was too large for one ruler. He set up the Tetrarchy, a system that split the empire into an eastern and a western half. The system soon collapsed, but the idea of a divided empire stuck.

paragraphs.heading: A new capital in the east
paragraphs.text: Constantine I won absolute power in 324. Over the following six years he rebuilt the town of Byzantium as a new capital he called "New Rome", later named Constantinople. He made Christianity legal, reformed the army and government, and introduced a stable gold coin, the solidus. Under Theodosius I, Christianity became the state religion, and over time Greek took the place of Latin in official business.

paragraphs.heading: Greatest reach and great losses
paragraphs.text: The empire was at its largest under Justinian I, who reigned from 527 to 565 and for a time won back much of Italy and the western Mediterranean coast. A plague that started around 541 and long wars with Persia then strained its money and armies. In the 630s and 640s Arab armies beat Byzantine forces in Syria and Egypt, and those provinces were lost for good. Africa followed in 698.

paragraphs.heading: Revival and fall
paragraphs.text: The empire steadied under the Isaurian dynasty and grew again under the Macedonian dynasty, enjoying a two-century renaissance. Civil wars and Seljuk raids later cost it most of Asia Minor, but it recovered in the Komnenian restoration. Constantinople stayed Europe's biggest and richest city until Paris passed it in the 13th century. In 1204 the Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople and broke the empire into pieces. The city was retaken in 1261, but the empire was only a regional power after that, and the Ottomans swallowed what was left until Constantinople fell in 1453.

paragraphs.heading: Romans, Greeks or Byzantines
paragraphs.text: Its people called themselves Romaioi, Romans, and their Muslim neighbours called the empire the "land of the Romans". After 800 AD, Western Europe called them Greeks instead, because the Pope and the medieval German emperors claimed to be Rome's true heirs. The word Byzantine comes from Byzantion, the Greek settlement on which Constantinople was built, and at first it described only the city's people. It is now the main term for the empire, though some modern historians say it should be dropped as unfair and inaccurate in origin.
